newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Rwanda tribunal slammed in U.N. investigation.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda tribunal slammed in U.N. investigation.

text.p: The Rwanda war crimes tribunal suffers from gross mismangement, underqualified staff, a weak prosecutor's office and benign neglect from U.N. headquarters, says a U.N. report released on Wednesday.

Unless the abuses were corrected, "the Rwandese will be right to suspect that justice delayed is justice denied," said the report prepared by Karl Paschke of Germany, the U.N.'s equivalent of an inspector-general, who heads the Office of Internal Oversight Services.
Set up in Arusha, Tanzania, the tribunal is to try leaders responsible for more than half a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus massacred in Rwanda in 1994 by Hutu troops and others.
The tribunal has indicted 21 people, seven of whom are held in Arusha. Another eight are at large and four are held in Cameroon. The U.S. and Switzerland hold one each.

Paschke did not mention any responsible officers by name but he used their titles, including the registrar in Arusha, the deputy prosecutor in Kigali and the departments of legal affairs and administration in New York.

Specifically, the report said that "not a single administrative area in the tribunal's registry functioned effectively." Finance had no accounting system, lines of authority were not clearly defined, internal controls were weak in all sections, and personnel were hired without the proper qualifications.

One employee kept silent about receiving a double salary accidently, still owes the United Nations $34,000 but had his contract extended until mid-1997 with the concurrence of the New York-based human resources department.
The registrar, Andronico Adede of Kenya, who controlled most administrative functions, spent half his time travelling without having his trips approved by anyone.
In one case a plane costing $27,000 was sent to pick up prisoners in a West Africa country, presumably Cameroon, but left empty because of no prior agreement with that country.

And in the Rwandan capital of Kigali, where the prosecutors office was located, an inexperienced staff as well as a lack of vehicles, computers, office equipment and appalling security marred the operation.

Paschke places some of the blame on the deputy prosecutor, Honoure Rakotomanana of Madagascar, who he says seconded more vehicles for his own use than needed and allowed investigators to follow their own legal strategy.

Former prosecutor Richard Goldstone of South Africa, whose job has been taken over by Louise Arbor of Canada, was also criticised for not insisting the Kigali office follow his instructions and indict national figures first.

Secretary-General Kofi Annan as well as his predecessor Boutros Boutros-Ghali had begun substituting personnel in Arusha when some of the abuses came to light last year and were publicised by the New York Times.

Paschke was critical of New York headquarters, particularly the legal affairs department run by Hans Corell of Sweden and the administration and management department run by Joseph Connor of the United States.
He said many problems were the result of a misperception of New York's responsibilities towards the tribunal, which was to function as an independent entity.
He noted New York had given assistance to the Hague-based U.N. tribunal investigating war crimes in the former Yugoslavia, but in Rwanda they "failed to provide adequate short-term support."
